comment:
* A stateful class that finds and extracts telephone numbers from {@linkplain CharSequence text}. * Instances can be created using the {@linkplain PhoneNumberUtil#findNumbers factory methods} in * {@link PhoneNumberUtil}. * *

Vanity numbers (phone numbers using alphabetic digits such as 1-800-SIX-FLAGS are * not found. * *

This class is not thread-safe.

variables.name: PATTERN
variables.comment:
* The phone number pattern used by {@link #find}, similar to * {@code PhoneNumberUtil.VALID_PHONE_NUMBER}, but with the following differences: *
    *
  • All captures are limited in order to place an upper bound to the text matched by the * pattern. *
      *
    • Leading punctuation / plus signs are limited. *
    • Consecutive occurrences of punctuation are limited. *
    • Number of digits is limited. *
    *
  • No whitespace is allowed at the start or end. *
  • No alpha digits (vanity numbers such as 1-800-SIX-FLAGS) are currently supported. *

variables.name: PUB_PAGES
variables.comment:
* Matches strings that look like publication pages. Example: * 
Computing Complete Answers to Queries in the Presence of Limited Access Patterns.
   * Chen Li. VLDB J. 12(3): 211-227 (2003).
* * The string "211-227 (2003)" is not a telephone number.

variables.name: SLASH_SEPARATED_DATES
variables.comment:
* Matches strings that look like dates using "/" as a separator. Examples: 3/10/2011, 31/10/96 or
   * 08/31/95.

variables.name: TIME_STAMPS
variables.comment:
* Matches timestamps. Examples: "2012-01-02 08:00". Note that the reg-ex does not include the
   * trailing ":\d\d" -- that is covered by TIME_STAMPS_SUFFIX.

variables.name: MATCHING_BRACKETS
variables.comment:
* Pattern to check that brackets match. Opening brackets should be closed within a phone number.
   * This also checks that there is something inside the brackets. Having no brackets at all is also
   * fine.

variables.name: INNER_MATCHES
variables.comment:
* Patterns used to extract phone numbers from a larger phone-number-like pattern. These are
   * ordered according to specificity. For example, white-space is last since that is frequently
   * used in numbers, not just to separate two numbers. We have separate patterns since we don't
   * want to break up the phone-number-like text on more than one different kind of symbol at one
   * time, although symbols of the same type (e.g. space) can be safely grouped together.
   *
   * Note that if there is a match, we will always check any text found up to the first match as
   * well.

variables.name: LEAD_CLASS
variables.comment: * Punctuation that may be at the start of a phone number - brackets and plus signs.

variables.name: text
variables.comment: The text searched for phone numbers.

variables.name: preferredRegion
variables.comment:
* The region (country) to assume for phone numbers without an international prefix, possibly
   * null.

variables.name: maxTries
variables.comment: The maximum number of retries after matching an invalid number.

variables.name: lastMatch
variables.comment: The last successful match, null unless in {@link State#READY}.

variables.name: searchIndex
variables.comment: The next index to start searching at. Undefined in {@link State#DONE}.

variables.name: regexCache
variables.comment: that use-case won't have a lot of benefit.
